To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) cognitive load is not a unitary construct, and that (2) cognitive load is a function of the interaction between the cognitive processes that are used to learn, the complexity of the material, and the learners' expertise.

(a) cognitive load theory can be strengthened by linking cognitive processes with processes used by biological evolutions; (b) complex learning requires a flexible adaptation of instruction to learners' needs, which in turn requires new methods to measure expertise development and cognitive load; (c) the complexity of real life tasks is often high, so that new methods to manage cognitive load are needed; and (d) complex learning is a long process that requires taking into account learners' motivational states.

(a) cognitive load theory can be strengthened by linking cognitive processes and evolution and that (b) the complexity, motivational state, and expertise level of real-life tasks should be taken into account when designing complex learning.
In summary, our research is concerned with
how cognitive load theory can be applied to complex learning in real life settings, and how it can be extended to include motivational and expertise aspects of learning.
the question of how people learn complex skills in real-world settings.
the question: How can we design instruction that will enable learners to deal with the complexity of real life tasks in a flexible and efficient way?

CLT has developed from a theory of cognitive load in learning to a theory of cognitive processes in complex learning and expertise development.
